error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> src/respond.rs:142:9
   |
142 |         reason
    |         ^^^^^^ expected `String`, found `&str`

error[E0599]: no method named `to_owned` found for reference `&Rule` in the current scope
  --> src/respond.rs:178:22

After tracing through the match arms in `evaluate()`, the type mismatch originates from the `haystack` helper returning a borrowed slice while `block_reason` expects an owned `String` for the final message. The `Rule::Custom(pattern)` variant is constructed from a `Vec<String>` earlier in `parse_rules`, but the closure passed to `.iter().find()` was comparing against `&str` without dereferencing, which is why the compiler flagged the second error at line 178. Fixing this requires either changing the return type of `haystack` to `String` everywhere it's used, or adding an explicit `.to_string()` at the three call sites in `evaluate`. I also noticed the `Rule::LongNoSummary` branch does not increment the `matched_rules` counter used by the metrics exporter, which would silently undercount that rule in the telemetry dashboard. There are two more warnings about unused `mut` bindings in `parse_rules` for the `rules` vector that aren't strictly related but showed up in the same build output.

diff --git a/serve/src/respond.rs b/serve/src/respond.rs
index 3a1b2c4..9f0e112 100644
--- a/serve/src/respond.rs
+++ b/serve/src/respond.rs
@@ -88,7 +88,7 @@ fn evaluate(reply: &str, rules: &[Rule]) -> Vec<Rule> {
-    rules.iter().find(|r| haystack(reply).contains(&r.pattern)).cloned().into_iter().collect()
+    rules.iter().filter(|r| haystack(reply).contains(&r.pattern)).cloned().collect()

The change from `.find()` to `.filter()` means every matching rule is now returned instead of only the first one, which is a behavioral change for any caller relying on early termination. The `parse_rules` function upstream sorts rules by a `priority` field before this call, so the ordering of the returned vector will now reflect priority rather than definition order, which could affect the `block_reason` formatting since it currently joins the first three matches with a semicolon. I checked the callers in `mcp.rs` and `cli.rs` and neither depends on receiving exactly one rule back, so this should be safe, though the footer rendering in `footer.rs` does format based on `matches.len() == 1` in one branch, which will now behave differently for replies matching multiple rules simultaneously.

De panic ontstaat doordat `block_reason` een `.unwrap()` aanroept op het resultaat van `rules.iter().find(...)`, wat `None` teruggeeft zodra de rulebook een regel bevat zonder `pattern` veld. Dat gebeurt specifiek wanneer iemand handmatig een nieuwe regel toevoegt aan de JSON zonder het verplichte veld in te vullen, wat blijkbaar is gebeurd bij de laatste handmatige edit van de rulebook. De `handle_stop_hook` functie in mcp.rs vangt geen panics op, dus de hele hook crasht en de Stop-hook slaat vervolgens over zonder enige melding richting de gebruiker, wat verklaart waarom er de afgelopen dagen soms helemaal geen blokkade optrad ondanks een overduidelijke overtreding. Een fix zou zijn om `.unwrap()` te vervangen door een `match` met een duidelijke fallback regel, of door de rulebook parser strikter te maken zodat een ontbrekend veld al bij het opstarten faalt in plaats van pas bij evaluatie.

The `Rule` enum currently has six variants, one per guard rule, each carrying a `Vec<String>` of trigger substrings that get lowercased and compared against the lowercased reply text inside `haystack`. The `parse_rules` function reads the JSON rulebook once at startup and caches the parsed rules in a `OnceLock`, meaning a change to the rulebook file on disk requires a full process restart of the serve binary before it takes effect, which is not documented anywhere in the README. The `evaluate` function iterates the rules in the order they appear in the JSON array and returns the first match rather than all matches, so if a reply happens to trigger both rule 1 and rule 4, only whichever rule appears first in the file will be reported back to the caller, and the other violation is silently dropped from the response. This has an implication for statistics gathered from production: any reported per-rule violation counts likely undercount rules that tend to co-occur with earlier rules in the file, since only the first match ever gets counted. Fixing this would mean changing the return type from `Option<Rule>` to `Vec<Rule>` throughout the call chain, which touches `mcp.rs`, `cli.rs`, and the footer rendering code as well.
